g11-history-uh9-t1.overview: The Industrial Revolution was the greatly increased output of machine-made goods that began in England in the mid-18th century and later spread to Europe and North America. This lesson explains its agricultural roots, the inventions that drove it, and the social changes it produced.
objectives: Explain why the Industrial Revolution began in England before anywhere else
Describe the agricultural changes that prepared the way for machine industry
Identify the main textile, steam and transport inventions and their inventors
Analyse the social effects of industrialization, including urbanization and class tension
Evaluate the positive and negative outcomes of the Industrial Revolution
g11-history-uh9-t1.simple: The Industrial Revolution was the huge rise in machine-made goods that started in England in the mid-18th century. Before it, people wove cloth by hand in workshops. An earlier Agricultural Revolution helped: landowners enclosed land, used the seed drill from about 1701 and practised crop rotation, so food and population grew. England also had coal, iron ore, rivers, harbours, banks and political stability. John Kay made the flying shuttle in 1733, James Hargreaves the spinning jenny around 1764, Richard Arkwright the water frame in 1769, Samuel Crompton the spinning mule in 1779, and Edmund Cartwright the power loom in 1787. James Watt improved the steam engine in 1765. Factories brought long hours, pollution and child labour, but also more jobs and a better standard of living.
g11-history-uh9-t1.detailed:
What the Industrial Revolution was. The Industrial Revolution refers to the greatly increased output of machine-made products that began in England in the mid-18th century. Before it, people wove textiles by hand in workshops; during it, machines began to replace manual labour. From England it spread to Europe and North America. The industries transformed were textiles, iron, mechanical engineering, chemical manufacturing, and transportation, mainly steamships and railways.

Agricultural roots. The Agricultural Revolution of the early 18th century paved the way. By 1700 wealthy landowners were buying up the land village farmers once worked and enclosing it with fences. Larger fields let them experiment with more productive seeding and harvesting. The seed drill, invented about 1701, sowed seeds in well-spaced rows at specific depths so more took root, and crop rotation kept the soil productive. Small farmers became tenant farmers or gave up farming and moved to the cities. As food supplies and living conditions improved, England's population grew, raising demand for food and clothes, and the farmers who lost their land became factory workers.

Why England first. England had a large population of workers and extensive natural resources: water power and coal to fuel machines, iron ore to build machines, tools and buildings, rivers for inland transportation, and harbours for merchant ships. Industrialization, the process of developing machine production of goods, needs exactly these. Britain also had an expanding economy, business people ready to invest in new inventions, and a highly developed banking system whose loans financed machinery. Growing overseas trade and prosperity increased demand for goods. Britain's political stability gave it an advantage over its neighbours: none of the wars of the 1700s was fought on British soil, Parliament passed laws to encourage business, and the country possessed all the factors of production, namely land, labour and capital.

Inventions that transformed textiles. In 1733 John Kay made the flying shuttle, a boat-shaped piece of wood to which yarn was attached, and it doubled the work a weaver could do in a day. Around 1764 James Hargreaves invented the spinning jenny, which let one spinner work eight threads at once. Richard Arkwright's water frame of 1769 used water power from rapid streams, and in 1779 Samuel Crompton combined the jenny and the water frame to make the spinning mule, which produced thread stronger, finer and more consistent than before. Edmund Cartwright's power loom of 1787 sped up weaving. These bulky, expensive machines were taken out of the home into factories built near rivers and streams, and in 1793 the American Eli Whitney invented the cotton gin, which multiplied the amount of cotton that could be cleaned.

Steam and transport. As early as 1705 coal miners were using steam-powered pumps to remove water from deep mine shafts, but these early engines wasted fuel. In 1765 James Watt, a mathematical instrument maker, worked out how to make the steam engine faster and more efficient while burning less fuel. Robert Fulton built the steamboat Clermont, whose first successful trip was in 1807. Canals, and better roads built by private companies with the work of the Scottish engineer John McAdam, improved transport. In 1804 Richard Trevithick invented a steam-driven locomotive, and in 1821 George Stephenson began work on the world's first railroad line, which opened the next year. Railways gave manufacturers a cheap way to move goods, created hundreds of thousands of new jobs for railroad workers and miners, helped agriculture and fishing reach distant cities, and encouraged country people to take distant city jobs.

Social costs and gains. The change to machine production at first caused human suffering: unhealthy working conditions, air and water pollution, child labour, and rising tension between the working class and the middle class. The average worker spent 14 hours a day on the job, six days a week; factories were seldom well lit or clean; machines injured workers, and there was no government programme to provide aid in case of injury. Coal mines were the most dangerous and made the average miner's life span ten years shorter than that of other workers, while many women and children were employed there as the cheapest source of labour. After 1800 the balance shifted from the countryside toward the cities, a process called urbanization. Some workers, the Luddites named after Ned Ludd, attacked factories in northern England from 1811 to 1816 and smashed the machinery they believed was putting them out of work. Yet the revolution also created jobs, contributed to the wealth of the nation, fostered technological progress, and raised the standard of living, bringing healthier diets, better housing, cheaper mass-produced clothing and expanded education.

New ideas about wealth. Laissez faire, French for let do, held that owners of industry should set working conditions without interference from governing bodies. Adam Smith defended this free market in his 1776 book The Wealth of Nations with what he called the three natural laws of economics: self-interest, competition, and supply and demand. French reformers such as Charles Fourier and Saint-Simon proposed socialism, in which the factors of production are owned by the public and operate for the welfare of all. Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels went further in The Communist Manifesto of 1848, dividing society into the bourgeoisie, the employers, and the proletariat, the workers.

A larger field fenced off by a wealthy landowner, in which more productive seeding and harvesting methods were tried.
The process of developing machine production of goods.
The resources an economy needs to produce goods: land, labour and capital.
City building and the movement of people from the countryside to cities.

An economic system in which the factors of production are owned by the public and operate for the welfare of all.

workedExamples.problem: Why did the Industrial Revolution begin in England rather than somewhere else in Europe?
workedExamples.given: England had coal and water power, iron ore, rivers and harbours, a large population of workers, a banking system that gave loans, overseas trade, and a government that protected business.
workedExamples.formula: Framework: industrialization requires the factors of production, land, labour and capital, together with natural resources, markets and political stability.
workedExamples.substitution: Checking England against the list: resources are present, labour is present because farmland was enclosed, capital is present through banks and trade, and the state protects business.
workedExamples.calculation: Because England was the one country that possessed every requirement at once, it industrialised first and then exported the process to Europe and North America.
workedExamples.answer: England began first because it alone combined natural resources, a large labour force, capital from banks and trade, and political stability.

workedExamples.problem: Show how the Agricultural Revolution helped to create the factory workforce of England.
workedExamples.given: Landowners enclosed land, the seed drill of about 1701 and crop rotation raised yields, food supplies and population grew, and small farmers lost their land.
workedExamples.formula: Framework: cause and effect, a change in one part of the economy produces a change in another.
workedExamples.substitution: Enclosure removed small farmers from the land; at the same time higher yields and a growing population created more mouths to feed and more hands seeking work.
workedExamples.calculation: The dispossessed farmers moved to the cities and became factory workers, while the larger population supplied both the labour and the demand for machine-made goods.
workedExamples.answer: Enclosure pushed farmers off the land and population growth created demand, so the countryside supplied the labour that the new factories absorbed.

workedExamples.problem: A weaver in northern England lost his livelihood after power looms arrived. Explain his reaction using the Luddite movement as evidence.
workedExamples.given: Machines replaced manual workers, wages fell, and from 1811 to 1816 the Luddites, named after Ned Ludd, attacked factories and destroyed labour-saving machinery.
workedExamples.formula: Framework: social consequences of technological change, in which displaced workers may resist the technology they blame for their unemployment.
workedExamples.substitution: The weaver's trade disappeared because a machine could do the work faster; he therefore saw the machine, not the market, as the cause of his poverty.
workedExamples.calculation: That reasoning explains why the Luddites broke machines rather than organising for political reform, so their violence expresses the human cost of early industrialization.
workedExamples.answer: The Luddite attacks show that early industrialization destroyed old skills and produced protest, even though it later raised the general standard of living.

workedExamples.problem: Compare laissez faire and socialism as answers to the suffering of industrial workers.
workedExamples.given: Laissez faire thinkers opposed minimum wage laws and better conditions, while socialists such as Charles Fourier and Saint-Simon wanted public ownership and a planned economy.
workedExamples.formula: Framework: comparison of two competing economic philosophies by their view of the role of government.
workedExamples.substitution: Laissez faire trusts the free market and leaves business alone; socialism trusts government control of factories, mines and railroads to end poverty and promote equality.
workedExamples.calculation: The two differ on who should act, the market or the state, and so they propose opposite remedies for the same poverty.
workedExamples.answer: Laissez faire lets owners decide, while socialism places ownership and planning in public hands for the welfare of all.

commonMistakes: Believing the Industrial Revolution began in the 1800s, when it began in England in the mid-18th century.
Thinking machines were invented before the agricultural changes that freed up labour and raised food supply.
Confusing the flying shuttle of John Kay with the spinning jenny of James Hargreaves.
Assuming that the Industrial Revolution benefited everyone at once, when workers suffered for decades first.
Believing that Britain's wars of the 1700s were fought on British soil, when none of them was.
Treating laissez faire and socialism as the same idea, when they hold opposite views on government interference.
Forgetting that the Industrial Revolution spread from England to Europe and North America, not the other way round.
applications: Explaining how Ethiopia's own shift toward manufacturing industry depends on the same factors of production described in the lesson.
Debating whether factories today should be allowed to set their own working conditions or be regulated by the state.
Tracing how a new machine or technology can create jobs in one place and destroy old livelihoods in another.
Discussing child labour laws in Ethiopia as a response to the suffering described in early English factories.
Using the enclosure example to explain why people migrate from rural areas to Addis Ababa and other cities today.
g11-history-uh9-t1.summary: The Industrial Revolution was the great increase in machine-made goods that began in England in the mid-18th century and then spread to Europe and North America. It rested on an earlier Agricultural Revolution, abundant natural resources, capital, labour and political stability, and it was carried forward by inventions in textiles, steam power and transport. It raised production and the standard of living, but it also brought long hours, pollution, child labour, urbanization and sharp class tension.

g11-history-uh9-t2.overview: Britain's thirteen North American colonies broke away after the Seven Years War and a decade of disputes over taxation and representation. This lesson follows the revolution from the Stamp Act to the Declaration of Independence and the surrender at Yorktown.
objectives: Describe the thirteen British colonies and the effect of the Seven Years War
Explain the Stamp Act and the colonial cry of taxation without representation
Trace the course of the revolution from Lexington to Yorktown
Explain how Enlightenment ideas shaped the Declaration of Independence
Assess the reasons for American success and the effects of the war
g11-history-uh9-t2.simple: In the 18th century Britain held 13 colonies in North America. After the Seven Years War ended in 1763, Britain needed money and passed the Stamp Act in 1765, taxing printed materials. Colonists protested taxation without representation. In 1773 they dumped British tea into Boston Harbour, and George III closed the port of Boston. The First Continental Congress met in Philadelphia in 1774, and the Second chose George Washington to lead an army. Fighting began at Lexington on April 19, 1775. On July 4, 1776 the Congress issued the Declaration of Independence, drafted by Thomas Jefferson on the ideas of John Locke. France entered the war in 1778 and helped trap the British under Lord Cornwallis at Yorktown in 1781, so the Americans won independence. The war freed the colonies and inspired revolutions in France and Latin America, but it did not abolish slavery.
g11-history-uh9-t2.detailed:
The colonies and the Seven Years War. In the 18th century Britain had 13 colonies in North America, while the French had also colonized parts of the continent throughout the 1600s and 1700s. In 1754 war erupted between the English and the French. The conflict was known as the Seven Years War, and the fighting lasted until 1763, when Britain and her colonists emerged victorious.

The tax dispute. Victory only led to growing tension. Great Britain had spent a huge sum of money on the war, and because the colonists had benefited from the victory, Britain expected them to help pay for its costs. In 1765 Parliament passed the Stamp Act, which required colonists to pay a tax to have an official stamp put on wills, deeds, newspapers and other printed material. American colonists were outraged because they had never paid taxes directly to the British government before. Colonial lawyers argued that the stamp tax violated colonists' natural rights and accused the government of taxation without representation: in Britain citizens agreed to pay taxes through their representatives in Parliament, but the colonists had no representation there, so they argued they could not be taxed.

From protest to fighting. In 1773, to protest an import tax on tea, a group of colonists dumped a large load of British tea into Boston Harbour. George III, enraged by the Boston Tea Party, ordered the British navy to close the port of Boston. Such harsh tactics worsened the relationship. In September 1774 representatives from every colony except Georgia gathered in Philadelphia to form the First Continental Congress, which protested the treatment of Boston. When the king paid little attention, the colonies formed the Second Continental Congress to debate their next move. On April 19, 1775 British soldiers and American militiamen exchanged gunfire in Lexington, Massachusetts, and the fighting spread to nearby Concord. The Second Continental Congress voted to raise an army and organise for battle under the command of a Virginian named George Washington. The American Revolution had begun.

Enlightenment ideas and the Declaration. The revolution was influenced by the Enlightenment, also known as the age of reason. Colonial leaders used Enlightenment ideas to justify independence, arguing that they had asked for the same political rights as people in Britain but the king had inflexibly refused, so they were justified in rebelling against a tyrant who had broken the social contract. On July 4, 1776 the Second Continental Congress issued the Declaration of Independence, drafted by Thomas Jefferson and firmly based on the ideas of John Locke and the Enlightenment. It argued for natural rights, stating that all men are created equal and are endowed by their Creator with certain unalienable rights, among them life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness. Since Locke had asserted that people had the right to rebel against an unjust ruler, the Declaration included a long list of George III's abuses and ended by declaring the colonies separated from Britain.

How the Americans won. Shortly after the Declaration the two sides went to war. At first glance the colonists seemed destined for quick defeat, since Washington's disparate, poorly trained army faced the well-trained forces of the most powerful country in the world. Several reasons explain the colonists' success. First, their motivation for fighting was much stronger than that of the British. Second, the overconfident British generals made several mistakes. Third, time was on the Americans' side, because fighting an overseas war 3,000 miles from London was terribly expensive and after a few years tax-weary British citizens called for peace. Finally, the Americans did not fight alone. Louis XVI of France had little sympathy for the ideals of the American Revolution, but he was eager to weaken France's rival, Britain, and French entry into the war in 1778 was decisive. In 1781 a combined force of about 9,500 Americans and 7,800 French trapped a British army commanded by Lord Cornwallis near Yorktown, Virginia. Unable to escape, Cornwallis eventually surrendered, and the Americans won their independence.

Effects of the war. The war brought about the liberation of the American people from British colonial rule and created an independent American nation that finally became the United States of America. It highly influenced the revolutions in France and Latin America. It did not, however, abolish the slavery system.

The 1765 law requiring colonists to pay a tax for an official stamp on wills, deeds, newspapers and other printed material.
The colonial complaint that Britain taxed them although they had no representatives in Parliament.
The 1773 protest in which colonists dumped a large load of British tea into Boston Harbour.
The gathering of colonial representatives, first in September 1774, that organised resistance and later voted to raise an army.
The document issued by the Second Continental Congress on July 4, 1776, drafted by Thomas Jefferson and based on John Locke and the Enlightenment.
The Enlightenment idea that government rests on agreement with the people, so a tyrant who breaks it may be resisted.

workedExamples.problem: Why did the American colonists claim that the Stamp Act was unjust?
workedExamples.given: The Stamp Act of 1765 taxed wills, deeds, newspapers and other printed material; the colonists had never paid taxes directly to Britain before and had no representatives in Parliament.
workedExamples.formula: Framework: the Enlightenment idea that legitimate government rests on the consent of the governed and the right of representation.
workedExamples.substitution: Applying that principle, a tax is lawful only when the taxed people agree to it through representatives, and the colonists had none.
workedExamples.calculation: Because they were taxed without any voice in Parliament, the colonists concluded that their natural rights had been violated.
workedExamples.answer: They called it taxation without representation and argued that it violated their natural rights.

workedExamples.problem: How did Enlightenment thinking appear in the Declaration of Independence?
workedExamples.given: The Declaration was drafted by Thomas Jefferson and based on John Locke; it spoke of all men being created equal and of unalienable rights to life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness; it listed George III's abuses and declared separation from Britain.
workedExamples.formula: Framework: the social contract and natural rights, which hold that people may rebel against an unjust ruler.
workedExamples.substitution: The colonists argued that the king had broken the social contract by refusing them the rights of British citizens.
workedExamples.calculation: Reading the document through Locke's ideas, the list of abuses is the evidence of a broken contract and the declaration of separation is the remedy.
workedExamples.answer: It applied Locke's natural rights and social contract ideas to justify independence from a tyrant.

workedExamples.problem: Why did the poorly trained American army defeat the most powerful country in the world?
workedExamples.given: American motivation was stronger, British generals were overconfident and made mistakes, the war was fought 3,000 miles from London, and France entered the war in 1778 and helped at Yorktown in 1781.
workedExamples.formula: Framework: analysis of the relative strengths of the two sides in war, including motivation, geography, cost and allies.
workedExamples.substitution: Weighing the factors, the Americans fought for their homes, the British fought far away at great expense, and French help supplied money, troops and naval power.
workedExamples.calculation: Together these factors outweighed British training and wealth, so the Americans could lose battles and still win the war.
workedExamples.answer: The Americans won because of stronger motivation, British mistakes, the cost of an overseas war, and decisive French help.

workedExamples.problem: The American Revolution is said to have been incomplete. Give the evidence.
workedExamples.given: The war freed the colonies from British rule and created the United States, but the textbook states it did not abolish the slavery system.
workedExamples.formula: Framework: evaluating a revolution by asking whose freedom it actually secured.
workedExamples.substitution: Applying that test, the language of equality in the Declaration applied in practice to white colonists while enslaved people remained in bondage.
workedExamples.calculation: Because slavery continued, the revolution enlarged liberty for one group without ending the enslavement of another.
workedExamples.answer: It was incomplete because it did not abolish slavery, even though it ended colonial rule.

commonMistakes: Confusing the Seven Years War, which ended in 1763, with the American war of independence.
Thinking the Stamp Act taxed tea, when it taxed printed materials such as newspapers and wills.
Believing France helped the Americans out of sympathy for their ideals, when Louis XVI mainly wanted to weaken Britain.
Mixing up the First and Second Continental Congress and what each one did.
Assuming the Americans won easily, when they were poorly trained and faced the strongest power of the day.
Thinking the Declaration of Independence was written by George Washington rather than Thomas Jefferson.
Believing the revolution abolished slavery, when it did not.
applications: Explaining why the principle of no taxation without representation still matters in modern parliaments.
Comparing the American fight for independence with Ethiopia's own struggle against colonial aggression at Adwa.
Debating whether a people ever has the right to rebel against an unjust ruler, and under what conditions.
Studying how foreign alliances, such as France's help to the Americans, can decide the outcome of a war.
Discussing how a founding document such as the Declaration can inspire later movements for rights.
g11-history-uh9-t2.summary: Britain's thirteen North American colonies rebelled after the Seven Years War because Parliament taxed them without giving them representation. Protest turned to war at Lexington in 1775, and on July 4, 1776 the Second Continental Congress issued the Declaration of Independence, drafted by Thomas Jefferson on the ideas of John Locke and the Enlightenment. Strong motivation, British mistakes, distance and French help brought victory at Yorktown in 1781; the war freed the colonies and inspired revolutions in France and Latin America, but it did not abolish slavery.

g11-history-uh9-t3.overview: The French Revolution destroyed the Old Regime of absolute monarchy and privilege and carried the ideas of liberty, equality and fraternity across Europe. This lesson traces its causes, its four phases, its reforms and the Reign of Terror.
objectives: Describe French society under the Old Regime and its three estates
Distinguish the long-term from the short-term causes of the French Revolution
Outline the four phases of the revolution
Explain the reforms of the National Assembly and the Declaration of the Rights of Man
Analyse the Reign of Terror and the rise of the Directory
g11-history-uh9-t3.simple: Under the Old Regime France was an absolute monarchy divided into three estates. The First Estate was the Catholic clergy and the Second Estate the nobility; both were privileged and paid no taxes. The Third Estate, peasants, artisans, city workers and the bourgeoisie, was the majority but unprivileged. Poor harvests, deficit spending by Louis XVI and the influence of the Enlightenment caused the revolution. On May 5, 1789 the Estates General met, and the Third Estate declared itself the National Assembly and took the Tennis Court Oath. On July 14, 1789 Parisians stormed the Bastille. The revolution passed through the National Assembly, the Legislative Assembly, the Convention and the Directory. Louis XVI was guillotined on January 21, 1793, and the Reign of Terror killed about 15,000 people before Robespierre fell on July 28, 1794.
g11-history-uh9-t3.detailed:
The Old Regime. The socio-political system that existed in most of Europe during the 18th century was known as the Old Regime. France was ruled by an absolute monarchy whose power was limited neither by constitution nor by tradition, and society was divided into the privileged and the unprivileged. The privileged paid no taxes and were treated well, while the unprivileged paid taxes and were treated badly. The French people were divided into three estates: the First Estate of high-ranking members of the Catholic Church, the Second Estate of the nobility, and the Third Estate of peasants in the countryside, artisans, city workers and wealthy bourgeoisie merchants in the cities. The First and Second Estates were privileged; the Third Estate was unprivileged but formed the majority.

Causes of the revolution. France's economy under the Old Regime was based primarily on agriculture, and peasant farmers bore the burden of taxation. Years of poor harvests left peasants in trouble paying their regular taxes, and the bourgeoisie were upset that they paid taxes while nobles did not. France was bankrupt because Louis XVI lavished money on himself and on residences like Versailles, while Queen Marie Antoinette was seen as a wasteful spender. The government's funds were also depleted by wars, including the funding of the American Revolution, and deficit spending, a government spending more money than it takes in from tax revenues, greatly damaged the economy. Worse still, the privileged classes would not submit to being taxed. The Revolution also drew heavily on the Enlightenment, the age of reason, whose philosophes used reason and logic rather than faith and superstition, questioned the divine right of kings, and asked how governments are formed. The textbook divides the causes into long-term causes such as absolutism, the unjust Old Regime, poor harvests, Enlightenment philosophes, mercantilism and the example of earlier revolutions, and short-term causes such as bankruptcy, the Great Fear, the worst famine in memory, and the meeting of the Estates General, which had not met since 1614.

The National Assembly, 1789 to 1791. In the winter of 1788 and 1789 preparations for the Estates General were under way. On May 5, 1789 the Estates General convened and each estate was given one vote, so the First and Second Estates combined their votes against the Third. The Third Estate demanded voting by population, which would give it a majority, and the disagreement produced a deadlock. The Third Estate declared itself the National Assembly, and when Louis XVI locked it out of the meeting it relocated to a nearby tennis court and vowed to stay together and create a written constitution, an event known as the Tennis Court Oath. On June 23, 1789 Louis XVI surrendered and ordered the three estates to meet together as the National Assembly and vote by population on a constitution for France. When news of his plan to use military force reached Paris on July 14, 1789, the people stormed the Bastille, the prison and symbol of French despotism, and seized weapons. An uprising spread; nobles were attacked, records of feudal dues and owed taxes were destroyed, and many nobles fled the country as emigres. On October 5, 1789 a group of women attacked Versailles and forced the royal family to relocate to Paris, where they spent several years in the Tuileries Palace as prisoners. The National Assembly abolished guilds and labour unions, ended special privileges, wrote the constitution of 1791, issued the Declaration of the Rights of Man, established equality before the law for men, reformed local government, and levied taxes based on the ability to pay.

The Declaration and the place of women. The Declaration of the Rights of Man guaranteed freedom of religion, speech and the press, property rights, liberty, equality and fraternity, the right of the people to create laws, and the right to a fair trial. The woman journalist Olympe de Gouges argued in her Declaration of the Rights of Woman that women are equal citizens and should benefit from governmental reforms just as men did, and Madame Jeanne Roland also led in the women's rights movement. Women did gain some rights during the Revolution, but these were designed for purposes other than liberating women: women could inherit property because doing so weakened feudalism, and divorce became easier because it weakened the Church's control over marriage. Other reforms seized, divided and sold church lands to peasants, required Church officials to be elected by the people with salaries paid by the government, and eradicated all feudal dues and tithes.

The Legislative Assembly and the Convention. The 1791 constitution formed a new government known as the Legislative Assembly, which lasted from 1791 to 1792. Its democratic features were that France became a limited monarchy, all laws were created by the Legislative Assembly, and feudalism was abolished; its undemocratic features were that voting was limited to taxpayers and offices were reserved for property owners. In June 1791 the royal family was caught trying to escape to Austria, and political parties, the major ones being the Girondists and the Jacobins, emerged. European monarchs feared that the revolution would spread, and France was invaded by Austrian and Prussian troops. In 1792 a new government, the Convention, came into being and stayed until 1795. It met for the first time on September 22, 1792 and established the first French Republic, a government in which the people elect representatives who create laws and rule on their behalf. Internally the Girondists, moderates representing the rich middle class of the provinces, were divided from the Jacobins, led by Marat, Danton and Robespierre, who represented workers; externally the monarchs of Austria, England, Holland, Prussia, Sardinia and Spain formed a coalition to invade France. The Convention abolished the monarchy, tried the royal couple for treason, and guillotined Louis XVI on January 21, 1793 and Marie Antoinette on October 16, 1793. Rouget de Lisle wrote the Marseillaise, the French national anthem, to inspire the troops, and after two years of fighting the external coalition was defeated.

The Terror and the Directory. The Reign of Terror lasted from September 5, 1793 to July 27, 1794 and brought huge material and human destruction. A Committee of Public Safety, headed by Danton and later by Robespierre, arrested those accused of treason and tried them before its Revolutionary Tribunal, and approximately 15,000 people died on the guillotine, which became known as the National Razor. Girondists who tried to end the Terror were themselves executed, and when even Danton wanted the executions stopped he too was tried and executed. Robespierre then led the Committee until the Convention turned on him and sent him to the guillotine on July 28, 1794, marking the end of the Terror. With the invaders defeated, the Constitution of Year III of the Republic in 1795 created the Directory Government, in which five directors were appointed by the Legislature and the Girondists defeated the Jacobins. Suffrage and the right to hold office were limited to property owners. The Convention had also adopted the metric system, abolished primogeniture, drawn up a comprehensive system of laws, ended debt imprisonment and slavery in France's colonies, and established a nationwide system of public education. The Directory, which lasted from 1795 to 1799, suffered from corruption and poor administration, and the people of France grew poorer and more frustrated, yet a strong feeling of nationalism, pride in the country and devotion to it, was fuelled by military successes, and this marked the end of the French Revolution.

keyTerms.def: The socio-political system of most of Europe in the 18th century, in which France was ruled by an absolute monarchy and society was divided into privileged and unprivileged.
The three orders of French society: the clergy, the nobility, and the commoners of the Third Estate.
The unprivileged but largest estate, made up of peasants, artisans, city workers and wealthy bourgeoisie merchants.
The wealthy merchants and middle class of the cities, who resented paying taxes while nobles did not.
A government spending more money than it takes in from tax revenues.
The vow of the Third Estate to stay together and create a written constitution for France.

workedExamples.problem: Why was France bankrupt on the eve of the revolution?
workedExamples.given: Louis XVI lavished money on himself and Versailles, Marie Antoinette was seen as a wasteful spender, the government funded the American Revolution, deficit spending drained the treasury, and the privileged classes refused to be taxed.
workedExamples.formula: Framework: fiscal crisis, in which government expenditure exceeds revenue and the wealthy refuse to contribute.
workedExamples.substitution: Adding the wasteful court spending and the cost of war to the refusal of the First and Second Estates to pay taxes leaves no way to close the gap.
workedExamples.calculation: Since taxation fell mainly on the poorest and the rich were exempt, revenue could not meet spending, and the state moved toward bankruptcy.
workedExamples.answer: France was bankrupt because of lavish royal spending, the cost of wars, and the refusal of the privileged classes to be taxed.

workedExamples.problem: What did the Third Estate demand at the Estates General, and why did the demand produce a deadlock?
workedExamples.given: The Estates General convened on May 5, 1789 with one vote per estate; the First and Second Estates combined their votes against the Third; the Third demanded voting by population.
workedExamples.formula: Framework: representation and voting rules decide who controls a decision-making body.
workedExamples.substitution: With one vote per estate the Third Estate could always be outvoted two to one, while voting by population would give it a majority because it was the largest estate.
workedExamples.calculation: The two sides wanted opposite voting rules, so no decision could be reached and the Third Estate broke away to form the National Assembly.
workedExamples.answer: The Third Estate demanded voting by population; the privileged estates refused, causing a deadlock and the birth of the National Assembly.

workedExamples.problem: Evaluate the Reign of Terror using the ideals of the revolution itself.
workedExamples.given: The Revolution proclaimed liberty, equality and fraternity and the rights of man, yet the Committee of Public Safety executed about 15,000 people between September 1793 and July 1794.
workedExamples.formula: Framework: measuring a revolutionary government against its own stated principles.
workedExamples.substitution: The Terror claimed to defend the Republic from traitors, but it imprisoned and executed suspects without valid evidence and finally consumed its own leaders, Danton and Robespierre.
workedExamples.calculation: Judged by the Declaration of the Rights of Man, the Terror contradicted the very rights it said it was protecting.
workedExamples.answer: The Terror betrayed the revolutionary ideals of liberty and fair trial, even though its leaders claimed to be defending the Republic.

workedExamples.problem: What did the constitution of 1791 make democratic, and what did it leave undemocratic?
workedExamples.given: France became a limited monarchy, all laws were created by the Legislative Assembly, feudalism was abolished, but voting was limited to taxpayers and offices were reserved for property owners.
workedExamples.formula: Framework: classification of a constitution by how widely it distributes political power.
workedExamples.substitution: Separating the popular features from the restricted ones shows that political rights were granted in principle but confined in practice to men of property.
workedExamples.calculation: Because the vote and public office were reserved for taxpayers and owners, the constitution was a step toward democracy rather than a full democracy.
workedExamples.answer: Democratic in ending feudalism and making the Assembly the lawmaker; undemocratic in restricting voting and office to property owners.

commonMistakes: Believing the Third Estate was a small minority, when it was the unprivileged majority of the French people.
Thinking the First and Second Estates paid heavy taxes, when they were exempt and privileged.
Confusing the Estates General with the National Assembly, which the Third Estate declared itself to be.
Placing the storming of the Bastille before the Tennis Court Oath, when the Oath came first in June 1789.
Assuming the Rights of Man gave women equal rights, when Olympe de Gouges had to demand them separately.
Thinking the Reign of Terror was directed only against nobles, when it executed revolutionaries such as Danton and Robespierre too.
Confusing the Directory, which lasted from 1795 to 1799, with the Convention, which lasted from 1792 to 1795.
applications: Comparing the three estates of France with social inequality in any society that taxes the poor more heavily than the rich.
Debating what liberty, equality and fraternity mean as political values today.
Explaining why people protest when a government spends beyond its means and refuses to tax the wealthy.
Studying the Declaration of the Rights of Man as an ancestor of modern human rights documents.
Discussing how a revolutionary government can slide into terror when it suspends fair trial and free speech.
g11-history-uh9-t3.summary: Under the Old Regime France was an absolute monarchy divided into three estates, with the privileged clergy and nobility exempt from taxes and the unprivileged Third Estate bearing the burden. Poor harvests, royal extravagance, deficit spending and Enlightenment ideas produced a revolution that began with the Estates General and the Tennis Court Oath in 1789 and passed through the National Assembly, the Legislative Assembly, the Convention and the Directory. It abolished feudalism and privilege and issued the Declaration of the Rights of Man, but it also produced the execution of Louis XVI and the Reign of Terror, which killed about 15,000 people before ending in 1794.

g11-history-uh9-t4.overview: Napoleon Bonaparte ruled France from 1799 to 1814 as Consul and then Emperor, reforming law, finance, religion and education while fighting almost constant war. This lesson covers his reforms, his campaigns, his fall and the Congress of Vienna that followed.
objectives: Explain how Napoleon Bonaparte rose to power and what the Consulate was
Describe Napoleon's main reforms, including the code of law and the Concordat
Trace Napoleon's major wars and the reasons for his defeat
Explain the decisions and principles of the Congress of Vienna
Evaluate the achievements and the limitations of Napoleon's rule
g11-history-uh9-t4.simple: Napoleon Bonaparte (1769-1821) was born on Corsica and became a brilliant artillery officer. He took power on December 25, 1799, ruling as First Consul from 1799 to 1804 and as Emperor from 1804 to 1814. His longest lasting reform was the code of French law, which gave legal unity and protected private property, and he also made the Concordat of 1801 with the Catholic Church, founded the Bank of France in 1800 and built a state system of public education. He won many victories and built the largest empire since Roman times, but he lost at Trafalgar in 1805, failed in Spain and in Russia in 1812, and was beaten at Leipzig in 1813. He abdicated in April 1814, returned for the Hundred Days in 1815, and was finally defeated at Waterloo and exiled to St. Helena, where he died in 1821.
g11-history-uh9-t4.detailed:
From soldier to ruler. Napoleon Bonaparte (1769-1821) was born of Italian descent to a prominent Corsican family on the French island of Corsica. Before he came to power he distinguished himself as a military genius specialising in artillery. He was a keen supporter of the ideals of the Enlightenment and the French Revolution, was associated with the Jacobins, and advanced rapidly in the army because of vacancies caused by the emigration of aristocratic officers. He took power on December 25, 1799, with a constitution giving him supreme power. The first part of his rule was the Consulate period from 1799 to 1804, during which he behaved more like an absolute ruler, governing France by demanding loyalty to the state, rewarding ability and creating an effective hierarchical bureaucracy. He may be thought of as the last and most eminent of the enlightened despots.

The code of law and other reforms. Perhaps the longest lasting legacy of Napoleon's rule is the code of French law, which provided legal unity and was the first clear and complete codification of French law, including a civil code, a code of criminal procedure, a commercial code and a penal code. It emphasised the protection of private property and gave rise to a strong central government and administrative unity. Many achievements of the Revolution were made permanent: equality before the law, with no more estates, legal classes, privileges, local liberties, hereditary offices, guilds or manors; freedom of religion; secularism, the separation of state and religion; property rights; and the abolition of serfdom. Napoleon also placed value on talent so that citizens could theoretically rise in government service according to their abilities, though he created a new imperial nobility to reward the most talented generals and officials, and wealth determined status. In religion he made the Concordat of 1801 with the Catholic Church, seeking to weaken the power of pro-Bourbon monarchs; under it the church would never lay claim to pre-revolutionary property, disloyal clergy were replaced with those who supported the state, and freedom of worship was granted. For financial unity he established the Bank of France in 1800, and the government established sound currency and public credit, provided food at low prices, increased employment, lowered taxes on farmers and made tax collection more efficient. Educational reforms were based on a system of public education under state control.

The limits of his rule. The drawbacks of Napoleon's reforms were severe. Women gained inheritance rights but were denied equal status with men: women and children were legally dependent on the husband or father, divorce was more difficult than during the Revolution, women could not buy or sell property or begin a business without their husbands' consent, the income earned by wives went to their husbands, and penalties for adultery were far more severe for women than for men. Workers were not allowed to form trade unions, and the state repressed liberty, subverted republicanism and restored absolutism through the creation of a police state. A spy system kept thousands of citizens under continuous surveillance, opposition was ruthlessly suppressed, and suspects were thrown into prison, if not executed without valid evidence. He also practised nepotism by placing his relatives on the thrones of nations he conquered.

War and empire. During the Consulate Napoleon fought many short wars with major European powers such as Britain, Austria, Sardinia and Russia, most often with Britain, and it was not until 1813 that the major European powers came together to fight France. The first of these wars was the Battle of the Nile in North Africa, where the British scored a victory, though Napoleon gained territory from Austria and Italy. His attempt to suppress a slave rebellion in Saint Domingue, Haiti, in 1804 was a fiasco, as Haiti defeated the French and achieved independence, and in 1805 France sold the Louisiana territory to the United States. The period from 1804 to 1814 was the Empire period, characterised by repeated war and defeat, and on December 2, 1804 Napoleon made himself emperor of France to prevent a probable return of the Bourbons. He viewed himself as a champion of freedom for subject peoples under the absolute rulers of Europe, and beginning in 1805 he engaged in constant warfare, eventually achieving the largest empire since Roman times, with France extending to the Rhine including Belgium and Holland, the German coast to the western Baltic, and the Italian coast down to Rome.

Defeat and exile. In 1805 Napoleon decided to invade Britain, a move seen as a major threat to the balance of power in Europe, so Austria and Tsarist Russia came to Britain's side. On October 21, 1805 the British navy destroyed the French and Spanish at the Battle of Trafalgar. By the Treaty of Tilsit, signed in June 1807, Prussia and Russia lost a considerable number of territorial claims, and Napoleon reorganised Germany by bringing 15 states together into the Confederation of the Rhine, which indirectly assisted the unification process. After Trafalgar he introduced the Continental System, which closed ports on the continent to British commerce, but it failed because in 1812 the United States came to support the causes of Britain and America's concern for British commerce, together with its own early infrastructural development, undermined the plan. The events after 1808 were not good for Napoleon: from 1808 to 1812 he fought the Spaniards who rejected his brother's candidacy for the Spanish throne and met with defeat, and in 1812 he invaded Russia and suffered a major defeat. In 1813 and 1814 he faced a coalition of Russian, Prussian, Austrian and British armies, and in October 1813 he was finally defeated at the Battle of Leipzig, also known as the Battle of Nations. He refused Metternich's Frankfurt Proposals, the Quadruple Alliance was created in March 1814 with each power agreeing to provide 150,000 soldiers to enforce peace terms, and Napoleon abdicated on April 4, 1814 after allied armies entered Paris. The Bourbons were restored under Louis XVIII, and by the Treaty of Paris signed on May 30, 1814 France surrendered all territory gained since the Wars of the Revolution began in 1792.

The Congress of Vienna and the Hundred Days. The Quadruple Alliance agreed to meet in Vienna, and the Congress of Vienna was held from September 1814 to June 1815, where representatives of the major powers met to redraw territorial lines and try to restore the social and political order of the old regime. Klemens von Metternich represented Austria and epitomised a conservative reaction to the French Revolution, opposing liberals and reformers because of the impact such forces would have on the multinational Hapsburg Empire. England was represented by Lord Castlereagh, who sought a balance of power by surrounding France with larger and stronger states. Prussia sought to recover territory lost to Napoleon in 1807 and gain land in northern Germany such as Saxony. Tsar Alexander I of Russia demanded a free and independent Poland with himself as king, and France was represented by Talleyrand, the French Foreign Minister. The principles of settlement were legitimacy, compensation and balance of power. Legitimacy meant returning to power the ruling families deposed by more than two decades of revolutionary warfare, so the Bourbons were restored in France, Spain and Naples, dynasties were restored in Holland, Sardinia, Tuscany and Modena, and the Papal States were returned to the pope. Compensation meant territorially rewarding those states which had made considerable sacrifices to defeat Napoleon: England received naval bases at Malta, Ceylon and the Cape of Good Hope; Austria recovered Lombardy and was awarded Venetia, Galicia and the Illyrian Provinces; Russia was given most of Poland with the Tsar as king, as well as Finland and Bessarabia; Prussia was awarded the Rhineland, three fifths of Saxony and part of Poland; and Sweden received Norway. The balance of power arranged the map of Europe so that never again could one state upset the international order and cause a general war. While the powers were busy at Vienna, Napoleon escaped from the island of Elba and entered France. He controlled power for one hundred days, from March 20 to June 22, 1815, having landed in the south of France on March 1 and marched into Paris with large popular support, seizing power from Louis XVIII, who fled. He defeated a Prussian army in Belgium on June 16, 1815, but his advance was finally halted at the Battle of Waterloo in Belgium in June 1815 by England's army led by the Duke of Wellington and Prussian forces. Napoleon was exiled to the South Atlantic island of St. Helena, far off the coast of Africa, where he died in 1821. His rule was the first egalitarian dictatorship of modern times, with lasting achievements and liabilities: on the positive side the consolidation of revolutionary institutions, the formation of a thoroughly centralised government, a lasting settlement with the church, and the spread of the positive achievements of the French Revolution to the rest of Europe; on the negative side the repression of individual liberty, the subversion of republicanism, the oppression of conquered peoples throughout Europe, and the enormous suffering caused by many wars.

workedExamples.problem: Why is Napoleon described as the last and most eminent of the enlightened despots?
workedExamples.given: He ruled as an absolute ruler with supreme power, yet he made the code of French law, the Concordat of 1801, the Bank of France in 1800 and a state system of public education, while repressing liberty and creating a police state.
workedExamples.formula: Framework: the enlightened despot, an absolute ruler who modernises the state while keeping power in his own hands.
workedExamples.substitution: Matching the evidence to the model, Napoleon's legal, financial, religious and educational reforms are enlightened, while his spy system and suppression of opposition are despotic.
workedExamples.calculation: Because he combined reform from above with unlimited personal power, he fits the model better than any ruler before him.
workedExamples.answer: Yes, because he modernised French law, finance, religion and education while ruling without sharing power or allowing liberty.

workedExamples.problem: Which of Napoleon's reforms lasted longest, and why does that matter?
workedExamples.given: The code of French law provided legal unity and was the first clear and complete codification of French law; it emphasised private property and made permanent equality before the law, freedom of religion, secularism, property rights and the abolition of serfdom.
workedExamples.formula: Framework: judging a reform by how long it survives the ruler who introduced it.
workedExamples.substitution: His empire and many of his conquests disappeared after 1815, but the legal code and its principles of equality before the law and property rights were carried into other countries.
workedExamples.calculation: Because the code outlived both his empire and the restored monarchies, it is the longest lasting legacy of his rule.
workedExamples.answer: The code of French law, because it gave legal unity and preserved key revolutionary achievements far beyond his rule.

workedExamples.problem: Explain why the Continental System failed to defeat Britain.
workedExamples.given: Napoleon closed continental ports to British commerce in an attempt to damage Britain's economy, but in 1812 the United States came to support the causes of Britain, and America's concern for British commerce together with its own early infrastructural development undermined the plan.
workedExamples.formula: Framework: economic warfare, which succeeds only if the blockade is complete and other states do not fill the gap.
workedExamples.substitution: Applying that test, Britain could still trade through the United States and other routes, so the closed continental ports did not stop British commerce.
workedExamples.calculation: Because the blockade leaked and American trade sustained Britain, the Continental System hurt continental economies more than it hurt Britain.
workedExamples.answer: It failed because Britain could still trade through other markets, especially the United States, so the blockade was never complete.

workedExamples.problem: What did the Congress of Vienna mean by legitimacy, compensation and balance of power?
workedExamples.given: Legitimacy restored deposed ruling families; compensation rewarded states that had sacrificed to defeat Napoleon; balance of power arranged the map of Europe so that no single state could cause a general war.
workedExamples.formula: Framework: the three principles of the Vienna settlement, applied to the decisions recorded in the textbook.
workedExamples.substitution: Under legitimacy the Bourbons returned in France, Spain and Naples and the Papal States were returned to the pope; under compensation England gained Malta, Ceylon and the Cape, Russia gained most of Poland and Finland, and Prussia gained the Rhineland.
workedExamples.calculation: Together the three principles aimed to restore the old order, reward the victors, and surround France with stronger states so that no power could dominate Europe again.
workedExamples.answer: Legitimacy restored old dynasties, compensation rewarded the victors with territory, and balance of power aimed to prevent any future general war.

commonMistakes: Thinking Napoleon became Emperor in 1799, when he became First Consul in 1799 and Emperor only on December 2, 1804.
Believing Napoleon's code granted women equal rights, when women were denied equal status with men.
Confusing the Battle of Trafalgar in 1805 with the Battle of Waterloo in 1815.
Placing Napoleon's defeat at Leipzig after his abdication, when he was defeated at Leipzig in October 1813 and abdicated on April 4, 1814.
Mixing up Elba, the island from which he escaped for the Hundred Days, with St. Helena, where he died in 1821.
Thinking the Congress of Vienna restored Napoleon, when its purpose was to restore the old regime and the Bourbons.
Assuming Napoleon allowed trade unions, when workers were not allowed to form them.
applications: Debating whether a leader who modernises a country but suppresses liberty is a reformer or a dictator.
Using the Congress of Vienna as an example of how states try to keep peace through a balance of power.
Discussing why a uniform written code of law is valuable in Ethiopia today.
Evaluating the human cost of war by weighing Napoleon's military glory against the suffering of many wars.
Comparing Napoleon's centralised administration with modern arguments about the power of central government.
g11-history-uh9-t4.summary: Napoleon Bonaparte (1769-1821) rose from artillery officer to First Consul in 1799 and Emperor in 1804, ruling as the last of the enlightened despots. His code of French law, the Concordat of 1801, the Bank of France and his public education system gave France legal, financial and administrative unity, while he denied women equality, banned trade unions and built a police state. Defeats at Trafalgar, in Spain, in Russia and at Leipzig forced his abdication in 1814, and after the Hundred Days he was beaten at Waterloo and exiled to St. Helena. The Congress of Vienna then settled Europe on the principles of legitimacy, compensation and balance of power.
